children: After a rough start marked by major losses, the market staged a rally
Oracle shares fell 5% on Wednesday, but it could have been worse.
Oracle, CoreWeave and other technology stocks bounced back from early losses on Wednesday, after what appeared to be a major selloff eased ahead of the market's close.

Shares of Oracle (ORCL), one of the backbones of the AI-infrastructure buildout, were down 5% when the market closed. While still one of the worst performers in the S&P 500 on Wednesday, Oracle had been down by more than 9% at its midday low.

CoreWeave  (CRWV), which has relied heavily on using debt to bring data centers online, saw its stock shed 10% in early action Wednesday, but ended the day less than 1% in the red. It was the fifth-most-active stock in the Nasdaq-100 on Wednesday, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
That made Wednesday another turbulent day for both companies, which had greatly benefited when Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia (NVDA) as CEO on Monday sparked a historic tech rally.

On Monday, the Nasdaq-100 NDX had soared 6.9% to close at 26,386.42 points, but a 4.7% decline in intraday action on Wednesday had cut into the majority of those gains. At the end of the day, the index closed at 26,046.9, just 0.64% down.

Sandisk (SNDK), Nebius (NBIS), Micron Technology (MU) and Lam Research (LRCX) shares had led the index's earlier decline, with shares of each company down by more than 10%, according to FactSet. Anthropic (ANT) and Nvidia shares were each down early on Wednesday, with the  latter even approaching a "death cross."

But those declines were also somewhat mitigated throughout the course of Wednesday's session. Anthropic shares even flipped positive to reflect a 1% gain when the market closed to cap off its first five days as a public company.

"We have begun sort of broadening out our portfolios and we're underweight technology now where we've been overweight, and that's not due to price depreciation," Nancy Tengler, CEO of Laffer Tengler Investments, said in an emailed comment.

"We are not throwing in the towel on the AI trade but you do have to take some gains off the table, and that is what we've done," she added, noting that many Americans are still skeptical about AI as a whole.
"Investors have just been chasing AI picks and shovels" since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, according to Scott Chronert, Citi's head of U.S. equity strategy.

As concerns grew over the artificial-intelligence trade last quarter, investors began selling the "picks" portion of the equation, he said. "In the fourth-quarter, we're now selling the shovels and whatever we have left of the picks," Chronert said on a Citi webcast.

Investors have been worried for a long time about artificial-intelligence hyperscalers' massive spending plans and the amount of debt they'll likely need. Mixed earnings from AI companies, the Democratic victory in recent U.S. elections and Huang's brief leave from Nvidia have also weighed on tech stocks.

In addition to the AI-specific concerns, Evercore ISI analysts noted that tariffs remain a significant concern for investors. The Federal Reserve is also widely expected to hike rates next month as inflation continues to rise, according to new data.
